title: Loose Parts
strapline: Pinecones, corks, pebbles and rings — nothing to break, everything to become.
intent: Think symbolically: a cork can be a boat, a person or a coin — the child decides, and can change their mind
Sort, classify and pattern by their own criteria — all the shiny ones, all the round ones, one of each
Feed transporting, enclosing and positioning schemas with materials that are made to be moved and arranged
Count, compare and subitise with objects that matter to the child in the moment
Refine fine-motor precision through picking, placing, threading and using tweezers and tongs
Own the outcome completely — there is no wrong way to arrange a basket of shells
implementation: Present loose parts in open baskets and sectioned tinker trays, sorted so every choice is visible at a glance
Resist naming what a thing "is" — follow the child's meaning, and let a pinecone be a cake all morning
Make your own transient arrangement alongside the child's, without ever improving theirs
Offer tools that up the precision: tweezers, tongs, scoops, muffin tins and picture frames for arranging inside
Spot schemas and feed them rather than stopping them — the child filling a handbag with pebbles is working hard
Add mirrors and empty frames to dignify arrangements as art; photograph favourites before tidy-up
Restock from your local walks — conkers, seed pods, interesting stones — so the collection keeps its story
key_questions: I wonder why you put all of those ones together?
What could this be in your game?
What comes next in your pattern?
Have we got enough shells to go all the way round the edge?
Where else could that one go — have you tried it?

impact.text: Children sort and group by their own logic — all the cars' "wheels", all the sparkly ones — and defend their categories.
Children match, sort and notice what's the same and different — two buttons that almost match are studied hard.
Patterns grow along frame edges and plate rims — cork, shell, cork, shell — and children extend them and predict what comes next.
Children see "three!" at a glance when pebbles land in a tray, without needing to count them.
Loose parts stand in for anything in pretend play — a pinecone cake for the shop, a curtain-ring steering wheel — and children narrate the game as they go.
Children choose their materials, mix them to see what happens, and arrange them their own way — the result is theirs and they know it.
Small hands grow precise: tweezers lift a single sequin, rings thread onto sticks, a pebble is placed exactly where it belongs.

enhancements: Tweezers, tongs and tiny bowls to turn arranging into a precision workout
Empty picture frames and mirror tiles as stages for transient art
Muffin tins, ice-cube trays and egg boxes that quietly invite one-in-each-space counting
A basket of curtain rings and dowels for threading, stacking and spinning
Story stones or a favourite picture book beside the collection to spark small-world retelling
A "treasure of the week" from a local walk — conkers in autumn, blossom in spring — so the collection follows the seasons

playing_exploring: Open-ended materials mean children play with what they know and stretch it — the same basket becomes shop, kitchen and rocket in one week
Children explore with all their senses: weight, shine, sound and texture all inform the choosing
active_learning: With no "finished" picture to match, children set their own goals and decide for themselves when it's done
creating_thinking: One object standing for another is early abstract thinking — the foundation for symbols, letters and numbers later on
Children make links between collections: what worked round the plate rim gets tried along the shelf edge
